name: Rotation Prediction (RotNet)
analogy: Think of it as a chart reader who is handed a candlestick picture that may have been turned upside down or sideways and must say which way it was turned. To answer, they have to know what a normal chart looks like, so practising on the turning puzzle teaches them how real charts are built.

steps.title: Collect unlabeled pictures
steps.description: The model needs only images, with no labels of any kind. In a trading setting the pictures are chart images, for example the last 60 bars drawn as candlesticks.
steps.inExample: Thousands of 64 by 64 pixel candlestick pictures of MNQ 5-minute windows, each showing 60 bars, are drawn from the lake.

steps.title: Turn each picture by a random quarter turn
steps.description: Each picture is rotated by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees, chosen at random, and the training code writes down which turn it applied. The answer key is manufactured automatically.
steps.inExample: One chart picture is turned by 180 degrees, so the price axis runs the wrong way and the newest bars sit on the left.

steps.title: Extract features with a convolutional network
steps.description: A convolutional network slides small windows across the picture and builds up features, from edges and candle bodies to the shapes of runs and gaps. The result is a feature vector describing the picture.
steps.inExample: The network turns the rotated chart into a vector of 256 numbers that describe candle shapes and the direction of the run.

steps.title: Name the rotation
steps.description: A small head reads the feature vector and gives a probability for each of the four turns. Telling the turns apart requires knowing that candles rise and fall in time from left to right and that tall wicks point outward.
steps.inExample: The head gives 88 percent to 180 degrees, 5 percent to 90, 4 percent to 270 and 3 percent to no turn.

steps.title: Score and adjust
steps.description: The probability given to the true turn is the score. Low probability on the true turn means a larger correction. This repeats across a huge pool of pictures until naming the turn becomes easy.
steps.inExample: The true turn was 180 degrees and the model gave 88 percent, a good score, so the adjustment is small.

steps.title: Discard the rotation head and keep the features
steps.description: The rotation head was only a means to an end. It is thrown away, and the network's features are reused for a real task, either by training a simple classifier on top or by fine-tuning the whole network on labelled pictures.
steps.inExample: A simple classifier on the 256 features is trained on 800 labelled chart pictures to tell breakouts from failed breakouts.

useFor.example: Learning general features from 200,000 unlabeled candlestick pictures before using 800 labelled ones to classify patterns.

useFor.task: Reducing the need for hand labelled chart patterns
useFor.example: Classifying double tops or head and shoulders shapes using only a small labelled set on top of the pretrained features.
Flagging pictures where the model cannot tell the turn easily, which can mark odd, irregular formations.
Feeding the features into the dashboard's chart pattern work as a starting point rather than training from random weights.

avoidWhen: Your input is a table of numbers or a sequence of bars; a window of bars has no quarter turn, so the method does not apply as designed, and a sequence model or tree model fits better.
You need a direct forecast of price or direction; the rotation puzzle teaches picture structure, and nothing in it is about where the market goes next.
A very simple cue lets the model solve the puzzle, such as a fixed price axis on a chart; it then learns nothing useful and the features are poor.

example.scenario: A research job draws the last 60 five-minute MNQ bars as a 64 by 64 candlestick picture, rotates it by 180 degrees for the practice puzzle, and later reuses the trained network to classify chart patterns.

input.summary: One chart picture, rotated by 180 degrees during training.

fields.name: picture size
fields.meaning: The number of pixels across and down in the chart image.

fields.name: bars drawn
fields.meaning: Five hours of trading shown as candlesticks in one picture.

fields.name: price range drawn
fields.meaning: The lowest and highest prices in the window, which set the vertical scale of the picture.

fields.name: rotation applied
fields.meaning: The turn chosen at random by the training code; the model is not told it.

fields.name: labels used
fields.meaning: The only answer key is the rotation the code applied itself.

output.summary: A probability for each of the four turns, and a feature vector kept for later use.

fields.name: probability the turn is 180 degrees
fields.meaning: The model's belief that the picture was turned upside down.

fields.name: probability the turn is 90 degrees
fields.meaning: A small share of belief on a quarter turn clockwise.

fields.name: probability the turn is 270 degrees
fields.meaning: A small share of belief on a quarter turn the other way.

fields.name: probability of no turn
fields.meaning: The share of belief that the picture is the right way up.

fields.name: feature vector
fields.meaning: The reusable description of the chart picture; this is the actual product.

example.reading: The four turn probabilities only show that the network has learned what a normal chart looks like. The product is the 256-number feature vector. Train a small classifier on it using your labelled patterns, compare it with the same classifier on a randomly initialised network, and treat any gain as an estimate to confirm out of sample.
